faqs.a: Most non-EU citizens need a work permit, usually Type A, plus a visa or residence title. The employer applies for the permit through the praca.gov.pl portal, and the worker then applies for a national Type D work visa at a Polish consulate. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no permit at all.
faqs.q: Do I need a work visa to work in Poland?

faqs.a: Type A is the standard permit for non-EU nationals employed by a Polish-registered company. It is tied to a specific employer and role, valid for up to three years and renewable. It authorises employment only, so a separate visa or residence card is still needed to stay legally in Poland.
faqs.q: What is a Type A work permit?

faqs.a: The labour market test was abolished under the Act of 20 March 2025, so employers no longer have to prove no local candidate could fill the role. However, a role on the local protected-professions list can still be refused in regions with high unemployment, and the employer must be in good standing with tax and social security authorities.
faqs.q: Is there still a labour market test in Poland?

faqs.a: Since 1 December 2025 the administrative fee is PLN 200 for work up to three months and PLN 400 for longer permits. The legal processing target is 30 days, but busy Voivodeship offices often take one to three months. Your salary must be at least the Polish minimum wage and comparable to local pay for the same role.

headline: Poland Work Visa Requirements 2026
metaDescription: Poland work visa requirements 2026: Type A permits, employer applications via praca.gov.pl, fees, processing times and salary rules for non-EU workers.

sections.content:
Non-EU citizens who want to work in Poland generally need two things: a work permit arranged by the employer and a visa or residence title that allows entry and stay. The most common route is the Type A work permit, issued for employment with a Polish-registered company and valid for up to three years. A single permit that combines work and residence rights is also available for longer stays.

EU, EEA and Swiss citizens can work in Poland without any permit. Ukrainian citizens under temporary protection can also work without a permit until at least 30 September 2026. Everyone else needs authorisation before starting work, and you cannot begin working before your visa start date.
sections.title: Who needs a Poland work visa?

sections.content:
The Type A permit is by far the most common route for foreigners employed by a Polish company, covering IT, construction, manufacturing and healthcare roles. It is tied to a specific employer and a specific role, so changing jobs means a new permit. The permit is issued by the Voivode, the regional governor of the Voivodeship where the employer is registered.

Poland also offers Type B permits for board members, Type C for intra-company transfers, Type D for posted workers and Type E for other cases, plus a seasonal Type S permit. Highly qualified professionals can instead apply for the EU Blue Card, which needs a salary of about PLN 13,355 gross a month in 2026 and offers stronger mobility and family rights.
sections.title: Types of work permits

sections.content:
Since 1 June 2025 all Type A applications must be filed electronically through the official praca.gov.pl portal; paper applications are no longer accepted. The employer, not the worker, files the application and must be a legally registered Polish entity in good standing with tax and social security authorities.

A major 2025 reform abolished the general labour market test, removing a former obstacle for most applicants. The new fee structure since 1 December 2025 is PLN 200 for permits up to three months and PLN 400 for longer ones. Once the permit is issued, the worker applies for a national Type D work visa at a Polish consulate, or a single residence-and-work permit through the MOS portal if already legally in Poland.
sections.title: How to apply in 2026

sections.content:
Your salary must be at least the Polish minimum wage, about PLN 4,666 to PLN 4,806 gross a month in 2026, and not lower than comparable local pay for the same role. The employer must also confirm the role is not on the local protected-professions list on the date of filing.

Processing typically takes one to three months at busy Voivodeship offices, so start early and confirm current fees and timelines with the competent office before filing. Poland's low unemployment rate of around 2.9 percent and moderate cost of living make it an increasingly attractive destination, but rules change often, so always verify against praca.gov.pl and the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs visa pages.
